finalText:
Both 301 and 308 mean the same thing: the resource has moved permanently. They differ in one way. When a client follows a 301, it is allowed to change a POST into a GET. When it follows a 308, it must keep the original method and body. Both are cacheable by default, and both are currently defined in RFC 9110.

**What each means.** RFC 9110 uses the same wording for both: the target resource "has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs" (301: §15.4.2, 308: §15.4.9, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). For both, the server SHOULD send a Location header with the new URI, and the client MAY follow it automatically.

**How the method and body are treated.**
- **301:** RFC 9110 says that "for historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request." If that is unwanted, it says to use 308 instead.
- **Why:** HTTP/1.0 originally defined 301 and 302 as keeping the method. Early clients disagreed on whether to resend POST as POST or as GET, and in practice they settled on GET. So 307 and 308 were added "to unambiguously indicate method-preserving redirects," and the text for 301 and 302 was changed to allow POST to become GET.
- **The general redirect rule:** a client following a redirect SHOULD resend the original request. It changes the method only if the status code's rules allow it. If the method becomes GET or HEAD, it removes content-related headers such as Content-Type and Content-Length, which means the body is dropped.
- **308:** it is the method-preserving version of 301. RFC 7538, which introduced it, says it "does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- **In practice:** following a 301, a POST may arrive as a GET with no body. Following a 308, the same method and body are resent to the new URI. MDN says "The request method and the body will not be modified by the client in the redirected request" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/308).

**The sources disagree on 301.** The same MDN page says that "A 301 Moved Permanently requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged," and treats switching to GET as something older clients get wrong. That conflicts with RFC 9110, which explicitly allows POST to become GET. The RFC is the normative text, so I've followed it. Elsewhere, the same MDN page describes 301 as a code "that may modify the request method when it is not a GET," which matches the RFC.

**Caching.** RFC 9110 calls both 301 and 308 "heuristically cacheable", unless the method definition or explicit cache controls say otherwise. RFC 7538 had described 308 as "cacheable by default."

**Where each is specified.**
- **301:** RFC 9110 §15.4.2.
- **308:** RFC 9110 §15.4.9.
- **Older documents:** RFC 9110 replaces (obsoletes) RFC 7231 and RFC 7538. RFC 7538 had itself replaced the experimental RFC 7238 without technical changes.
- **Deployment caveat:** RFC 9110 notes that 308 is "much younger (June 2014)" than the other redirect codes and "might not be recognized everywhere." RFC 7538 warns that a client that doesn't recognize 308 treats it like 300 (Multiple Choices), so automatic redirection isn't guaranteed.
